children: The following are expectations for the resumption of grain and soy complex trading at the Chicago Board of Trade at 8:30 a.m. CDT (1330 GMT) on Tuesday.
WHEAT - Down 8 to 11 cents per bushel
lower on a stronger dollar and hopes that diplomacy would halt Russian and Ukrainian attacks that have disrupted Black Sea grain exports.

U.S. President Trump on Monday announced that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop strikes on each other's energy facilities. The statement revived hopes of de-escalation in the war, though Russia and Ukraine both set conditions for accepting an energy truce.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture on Monday said that 8% of the U.S. winter wheat crop was planted as of September 13, lagging the five-year average pace of 12%. The agency said 93% of U.S. spring wheat was harvested as of Sunday, slightly ahead of the average pace of 92%.

CBOT December soft red winter wheat (WZ26) was last down 9-1/2 cents at $7.12-1/2 per bushel. K.C. December hard red winter wheat (KWZ26) was down 12-3/4 cents at $7.79-3/4 a bushel. Minneapolis December spring wheat (MWEZ26) was last 5-1/4 cents lower at $7.31 a bushel.
CORN - Down 2 to 5 cents per bushel
futures lower on a stronger dollar and after the USDA reported an unexpected improvement to U.S. crop conditions. Concerns about Midwest harvest delays limited declines.

The USDA on Monday raised its rating for U.S. corn in good-to-excellent condition by 1 percentage point. Analysts polled by Reuters, on average, expected a 1 point drop. The USDA also said 8% of the corn crop was harvested as of Sunday, ahead of the five-year average of 6%.
Forecasters expect heavy rain across parts of the Midwest this week, potentially slowing fieldwork in top corn producer Iowa.
CBOT December corn (CZ26) was last down 5 cents at $5.28-1/4 per bushel.
SOYBEANS - Down 3 to 6 cents per bushel

lower in a technical retreat from Monday's gains and spillover pressure from lower corn and wheat. Losses limited by steady demand from China and concerns about a rain-delayed harvest in parts of the U.S. Midwest.

The USDA on Monday left its weekly rating for U.S. soybeans in good-to-excellent condition unchanged at 58%, in line with trade expectations. The USDA also said 6% of the soybean crop was harvested as of Sunday, ahead of the five-year average of 3%.

The National Oilseed Processors Association is due to release its August U.S. crush report later on Tuesday. Analysts polled by Reuters, on average, expect last month's crush to dip to 211.553 million bushels, a three-month low.
CBOT November soybeans (SX26) were last down 5-1/2 cents at $12.98-3/4 per bushel.
